title: Three-qubit nonlocality paradoxes: beyond GHZ
authors: Nadish de Silva, Santanil Jana, Ming Yin
abstract: Quantum nonlocality paradoxes, such as that of GHZ, provide maximally sharp logical obstructions to classical probabilistic models of quantum correlations. They are key resources in a broad variety of information-theoretic tasks that exhibit unconditional quantum advantage. For example, in nonlocal games, which are communication tasks that serve as core technical tools in recent landmark results in quantum computational complexity theory.   Their role in establishing quantum advantage motivated their study by Abramsky et al. who introduced an infinite family of three-qubit paradoxes exhibiting novel conditional structure. This was later extended by de Silva et al. into a full classification program.   In this work, we completely classify all three-qubit nonlocality paradoxes established via a biconditional parity proof; this is a very large class of paradoxes that encompasses all earlier-known examples. We do this by introducing a suite of new structural and combinatorial techniques. We find that the landscape of nonlocality paradoxes is far richer than previously understood, violating regularity conditions underlying all prior constructions.
summary: The paper rigorously classifies three-qubit nonlocality paradoxes by developing advanced graph-theoretic and combinatorial techniques. It demonstrates that these paradoxical structures are far more abundant than previously believed, overturning restrictive assumptions about the necessary form of such paradoxes.
main_problem: To completely classify all three-qubit nonlocality paradoxes established via a biconditional parity proof, extending beyond previously known examples like the GHZ paradox.
main_result: The authors provide a complete structural classification for these paradoxes, showing that the landscape of nonlocality is much richer than previously thought by identifying new exotic paradoxes.
method: The work employs graph-theoretic formalisms (2-CNF formulae and implication graphs) combined with combinatorial techniques to map the set of specifications ($	ext{BPP}$) to a canonical data structure ($	ext{CanonicalTriples}$).
model_or_system: The focus is on three-qubit quantum systems exhibiting 'nonlocality paradoxes,' which are logical obstructions to classical probabilistic models arising from restricted joint measurability contexts.
key_observables: Nonlocal fraction, the existence of a witness path in the implication graph $I_{\Psi}(z)$, and the structure of the associated biconditional parity proof.
important_parameters: The number of qubits (fixed at three), measurement settings $\{M\}$, and parameters defining the entangled state $|	ext{B}(\lambda, \Phi)angle$.
main_assumptions: Initially relied on five restrictive assumptions; later work drops these to show a richer structure. Specific analyses focus on interpolant states or restricted Charlie measurements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry of balanced states and schematic forms of equations relating measurement angles $(	ext{A}, 	ext{B}, 	ext{C})$ to target directions, alongside implication graphs for specific examples.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining contextuality and nonlocality in three qubits (Chunk 2), establishing the link between paradoxes and biconditional parity proofs using graph theory (Chunk 3), developing a structural classification via 'Charlie clocks' (Chunk 4), presenting counterexamples outside interpolant states (Chunk 5), and finally confirming paradoxicality through detailed analysis of witness paths in implication graphs for various scenarios (Chunks 6, 7, 8).
why_interesting: This work provides deep structural insights into the limits of local realism in multipartite quantum systems, which is foundational knowledge for understanding genuine quantum advantage.
